newsitem.title: USA: Miami GOs cut to 'junk' in fiscal crisis.
newsitem.headline: Miami GOs cut to 'junk' in fiscal crisis.

text.p: Miami's bond rating was slashed to "junk" status on Wednesday after Mayor Joe Carollo declared a fiscal emergency and told Florida's governor he would welcome a state takeover of the financially troubled city.
Standard & Poor's Corp cut its rating for Miami's general obligation bonds to "B" from "BBB."
The cut means the bonds should be considered "predominantly speculative."
S&P said the rating could be cut further if the city files for bankruptcy, a possibility mentioned by the mayor but rejected as premature.

Carollo formally declared a fiscal emergency during a meeting late Tuesday in Tallahassee with the governor. The declaration could allow the governor to appoint a financial emergency board to take over fiscal management of the city, something no Florida governor has ever done.

"The mayor basically told the governor that they meet the criteria for financial emergency. This does not mean that the state will take over," Chiles' spokeswoman Karen Pankowski said. "It means the governor has certain authorities and we have some options."

Chiles' other options include requiring state approval of the city budget, authorizing a loan to the city, prohibiting Miami from issuing new debt, reviewing city records, and providing technical assistance.

Pankowsi said state officials were reviewing how other states handled in similar situations. Miami has a $68 million shortfall in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct 1. City commissioners are scheduled to vote Dec 12 on a bailout plan aimed at keeping it operating past February or March, when current funds run out.
"We've obviously never had anything quite like this in Florida," Pankowski said.
Carollo, who was not available for comment Wednesday, told The Miami Herald after the meeting with Chiles that he was "not at all opposed to having an advisory board."

"If anything it might be refreshing," Carollo told the newspaper. "When New York went thorugh its problems, the governor there put in an oversight board and look at New York -- it came back stronger than ever. We need to rebuild Miami top to bottom and change the Third World system that was running this city for so long."
Carollo also told the newspaper he had discussed with Chiles the possibility of declaring bankruptcy under Chapter 9 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, but that the move would be premature.

John Incorvaia, a vice president for municipal finance at Moody's Investors Service, agreed bankruptcy would be premature but said it was significant that the mayor had uttered the word publicly for the first time. The bond rating firm advised investors of the move Wednesday, but did not lower its Baa rating for the city's bonds, a rating that indicates "neither highly protected nor poorly secured."
"We needed to point out to people that now they're starting to refer to the word 'bankruptcy' and that's always a concern," Incorvaia said.

Orange County, Calif., filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy in the nation's largest municipal bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
Miami has not updated estimates of its deficit, which Carollo said exceeded the previously disclosed $68 milliom.

"Some politically hard decisions are gong to have to be made over the next month or so," Incorvaia said. "Even though the word 'bankruptcy' has been mentioned and is always a viable action, we're still looking for them to try to solve the situation."
The deficit was discovered after the former city manager and former finance director resigned to face criminal corruption charges.
